subtopics.title: Wave graphs: signed phase translation and inverse timing
subtopics.learning_goal: Interpret spatial displacement snapshots, translate phase patterns, and resolve or prove ambiguity in inverse timing.

qrt_targets.protected_work: Translate the signed spatial displacement field through a noninteger number of wavelengths while retaining the fixed-coordinate particle reading.
qrt_targets.decisive_route: A right-moving sinusoidal displacement wave has λ=0.60 m and amplitude 4 mm; at t=0 a crest lies at x=0.15 m. Its speed is 250 m/s. Draw the profile on 0≤x≤1.2 m at t=0 and t=3 ms, label extrema and zero crossings, and state the displacement at x=0.15 m at the later instant. Shortest valid route: Shift=+0.75 m, equivalent to +0.15 m. Later crests are x=0.30,0.90 m; troughs 0,0.60,1.20 m; zero crossings 0.15,0.45,0.75,1.05 m. At x=0.15 displacement is zero. Initial crests 0.15,0.75; troughs 0.45,1.05; zeros at 0,0.30,0.60,0.90,1.20.

qrt_targets.decisive_route: Three snapshots of one uniform sinusoidal wave have wavelength 0.80 m. At t=0 a crest set is x=0. At 5 ms it is x=0.20 m modulo 0.80 m. The magnitude of velocity is between 100 and 500 m/s. At 1.5 ms the crest set is x=0.54 m modulo 0.80 m. Infer direction, speed and period; establish uniqueness within the stated bounds. Shortest valid route: u=(0.20+0.80n)/0.005. Allowed n=−3,−2,−1,1,2 produce −440,−280,−120,200,360 m/s. Predicted offsets at 1.5 ms modulo 0.80: 0.14,0.38,0.62,0.30,0.54 m. Only +360 fits. T=0.80/360≈2.22 ms. The nearest marker alone would suggest +40 m/s, excluded.

qrt_targets.protected_work: Establish what identical periodic snapshots do and do not prove about pattern propagation, using counterexamples and independent evidence.
qrt_targets.decisive_route: Two spatial snapshots of an extended sinusoidal wave with λ=0.48 m, separated by 4 ms, agree at every x. A technician claims the disturbance did not propagate; another claims that all particles moved by 0.48 m. Given that |u| is between 100 and 300 m/s, assess both claims, enumerate compatible velocities and state a measurement that would resolve them. Shortest valid route: Identical profiles imply uΔt=nλ, so u=120n m/s. Bounds allow ±120 and ±240; neither no propagation nor bulk displacement follows. Individual displacement is bounded by amplitude. Independent direction plus a speed measurement, or a third snapshot at a nonredundant time, can resolve candidates; e.g. 1 ms offsets 0.12,0.24,0.36,0.24 distinguish some but not both ±240, so choose 0.5 ms giving distinct offsets 0.06,0.12,0.42,0.36 m.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Distinguish stationary pattern, periodic translation and material displacement as competing explanations.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate identical graphs into integer-wavelength condition.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Derive candidate family, filter bounds, evaluate claims, propose discriminating evidence.

algebra_computational_load.evidence: Arithmetic is incidental to the logical argument.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Identical observations do not imply no motion; periodic alias is decisive.

science_records.claim: A uniform travelling wave translates its spatial field by signed velocity times elapsed time; periodic phase markers are defined modulo wavelength.
assumptions: Uniform stationary medium; one stable travelling sinusoidal field
Snapshot times, phase identity and wavelength known
conditions_and_limits: Uniform stationary medium, one stable travelling sinusoidal displacement wave; signed pattern velocity is constant in each task.
The vertical graph coordinate is longitudinal displacement along the propagation axis, not a transverse particle path; pressure and displacement profiles are different fields.
A periodic snapshot identifies shifts only modulo the wavelength; a unique speed requires additional information.
A stationary sensor's time trace and a spatial snapshot are not interchangeable; no bulk particle transport is inferred.
Phase shift convention: positive signed shift is toward increasing x. Only a uniform repeating pattern returns after whole wavelengths.
science_records.units_and_signs: D and x in m (D often mm); u signed in m/s; t in s; λ positive in m; f=|u|/λ.

core1a.phenomenon: A travelling periodic profile may look unchanged at a later time although energy propagates.
core1a.scientific_narrative:
A snapshot of a travelling longitudinal sound wave can display each particle's signed displacement from equilibrium against its equilibrium position x. The vertical coordinate is a graph value, not the physical vertical position of the particle. A pressure snapshot instead records excess pressure. They are not the same physical quantity and their extrema need not coincide. Both may be periodic in the simple sinusoidal model; select the variable before interpreting any graph. The amplitude of a displacement wave is its maximum absolute displacement from equilibrium. Peak-to-peak distance on the vertical scale is twice that amplitude. Horizontal spacing of matching phase points determines wavelength; a crest and neighbouring trough are half a wavelength apart.

A useful way to reason is to imagine a transparent tracing of the snapshot. If a pattern moves right at constant speed v, after time t the tracing has shifted right by vt; if the signed velocity u is negative, shift left. The field value at a fixed coordinate x is the value originally at x−ut. Thus D(x,t)=D(x−ut,0). This is a statement about propagation of a pattern; one parcel of air does not travel at the wave speed. For example, a wave pattern can move metres while the local displacement amplitude is millimetres. In a sinusoidal profile, a crest initially at x0 has equivalent crests at x0+nλ, where n is any integer; after t their coordinates are x0+ut+nλ. This construction separates the travelling pattern from local oscillation.

An integer-wavelength translation reproduces the same graph at every coordinate. That does not mean the wave stopped. A half-wavelength shift changes a sinusoid's sign; a quarter-wavelength shift moves zero crossings to extrema. If a right-moving wave advances 1.5 wavelengths, the observable snapshot shift can be represented by half a wavelength, although the actual propagation distance was larger. A finite isolated pulse does not have this periodic ambiguity: its unique labelled feature can be followed directly.

The inverse problem is harder. Two snapshots showing equivalent phase markers at x1 and x2 give possible signed shifts x2−x1+nλ, not necessarily the smallest visible separation. For a time interval Δt, possible velocities are (x2−x1+nλ)/Δt. A declared speed range excludes candidates that violate it. An independent third snapshot at a different time tests the remaining candidates: compute where the same phase set would be and compare with the observation modulo λ. If more than one remains, report the ambiguity instead of guessing. A fixed detector's known period or an independently measured direction may also constrain the solution. Measurement uncertainty broadens the possible ranges and may prevent unique identification. These inverse constructions extend, rather than copy, a currently available Core2 wave-snapshot candidate.

In a laboratory, label axes and units, identify same-phase features, record propagation direction if known, and distinguish measured intervals from assumed numbers of cycles. A complete solution checks the sign of translation, units of distance and time, and the relevant periodic boundary. An independent check uses another phase marker or time observation, not repetition of the same arithmetic.

derivation_steps.action: Identify field and same-phase spatial interval.
derivation_steps.why_valid: The graph axes distinguish longitudinal displacement from physical geometry; repeated phase establishes λ.

derivation_steps.action: Translate all phase families by the signed pattern shift uΔt.
derivation_steps.why_valid: A travelling field is D(x,t)=D(x−ut,0), not a particle trajectory.

derivation_steps.action: For an inverse problem enumerate shifts differing by nλ and apply the speed range.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Periodic repetition makes all those shifts observationally equivalent in two snapshots.

derivation_steps.action: Test remaining candidates against an independent observation and report nonuniqueness if necessary.
derivation_steps.why_valid: An additional time or phase constraint may reject aliases; it does not guarantee uniqueness.

progressive_examples.problem: A displacement snapshot has a crest at x=0.12 m, the adjacent trough at x=0.32 m, and maximum displacement 3 mm. Give λ and peak-to-peak displacement.
progressive_examples.independent_check: The next crest is at 0.52 m; the two crest positions differ by 0.40 m.

progressive_examples.problem: A sinusoidal pattern with λ=0.50 m moves left at 300 m/s. A crest starts at x=0.10 m. After 2.5 ms, list crest coordinates in 0≤x<1 m.
progressive_examples.reasoning: Shift is −0.75 m, so the crest family is −0.65+0.50n m; visible crests are 0.35 and 0.85 m.
progressive_examples.independent_check: The shift modulo λ is −0.25 m (equivalent to +0.25); original crests at 0.10 and 0.60 become 0.35 and 0.85.

progressive_examples.problem: A periodic snapshot has λ=0.50 m. After 4 ms the crest set appears displaced +0.10 m modulo λ. A speed instrument bounds |u| between 80 and 300 m/s. After 1 ms the crest offset is +0.40 m modulo λ. Find u.
progressive_examples.reasoning: Candidates from first pair: (0.10+0.50n)/0.004; n=1 gives 150, n=2 gives 275, n=−1 gives −100, n=−2 gives −225 m/s; n=0 gives 25 outside range. At 1 ms the respective offsets modulo 0.50 are 0.15, 0.275, 0.40, 0.275. Only −100 matches.
progressive_examples.independent_check: At 4 ms −100×0.004=−0.40 m, equivalent to +0.10; at 1 ms −0.10 m is equivalent to +0.40.

figures.reasoning_step: Coordinate periodic spatial profiles at successive times and expose the translation ambiguity.

misconception.wrong_model: The same snapshot implies a stationary wave pattern; the nearest crest identifies the same physical particle.
misconception.diagnostic: Can a periodic profile reproduce itself while a disturbance continues to propagate? What would a marked particle do?
misconception.repair: Use a signed translation of the field and a family of equivalent phase positions. A marked particle oscillates locally; additional observations may be needed to determine the pattern shift.

exit_check.task: A wave with λ=0.60 m has identical profiles 3 ms apart. If its rightward speed is between 150 and 500 m/s, what speeds remain possible?
exit_check.reasoning: u(0.003)=n(0.60), so u=200n m/s, with n=1 or 2 under the given bounds.

stages.diagnose: Inspect the sign of the shift, the interval between phase markers, and the fixed-coordinate reading; identify the first inconsistency.
stages.repair: Shift every phase marker by the signed propagation distance, then use periodic repetition to place the field in the viewing window. Read the value at the specified coordinate.
stages.boundary_test: If the speed were 800/3 m/s at the same elapsed time, what would the later profile look like?
